reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is a programming lesson that builds and tests a Uniswap token-sniping bot with scripts, a sample pool and a small WETH swap. The speaker supplies project code and explicitly says the strategy is not guaranteed profitable; a separate bootcamp invitation is ordinary educational promotion rather than a deceptive trading-return offer.

opening.argument: Judge the invitation and the action together. The speaker introduces coding as a way to build bots that earn money, then offers to show viewers a bot that buys newly listed cryptocurrencies automatically. The tutorial goes beyond describing an idea: it identifies an amount to spend on each new token. That makes the earning possibility a reason to configure a trading bot and put assets at risk, even though no particular return is promised.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The sample swap demonstrates that the bot can execute a purchase; it does not demonstrate that buying a newly listed token earns money. Nor does providing code sever the connection between the opening income pitch and the later spending configuration. The profitability warning limits the claim, but arrives after the viewer has been shown a working purchase.

The completed swap is on a test copy of the blockchain, not evidence that viewers earned money or were asked to deposit into a scheme.

opening.argument: Several risk signals converge in the actual workflow. The bot is designed to buy as soon as a new pool appears, without a token-quality check described in the demonstrated event-to-swap sequence. The speaker sets a WETH spending amount, then raises slippage for the tutorial. He also warns that a displayed mnemonic could let someone steal money from a wallet holding real cryptocurrency. These details matter together: the viewer is being walked through automated, time-sensitive trading with both asset-spending and credential risks, not merely shown a diagram.

rebuttal.rebuttal: A small completed swap establishes execution, not safety or profit. Publishing code likewise lets viewers inspect the mechanism but does not remove the risks of an automatic purchase on a new-pair event. The speaker's warning about profitability reinforces that the demonstrated transaction cannot substantiate the earlier suggestion that such bots can earn money.

opening.argument: The lesson also serves as a funnel into participation. Its opening links bots to earning money, asks viewers to watch the whole tutorial, and directs interested viewers to a bootcamp. The description places that bootcamp alongside the project code, while the lesson walks through starting a bot that listens for new pairs and purchasing a token. A judge should weigh the tutorial as a whole: the educational format makes the proposed trading workflow approachable and gives viewers a route to continue with the presenter, rather than leaving the income idea as abstract commentary.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense separates the bootcamp invitation from the trading demonstration, but the speaker connects them: he says this project was first made for his community and urges viewers who want more to sign up. The later disclaimer does not erase that promotional path; it only concedes the trading strategy may fail. Code availability shows what is being promoted, not that the promotion is incidental.

The presenter explains the event listener and swap logic, demonstrates them on a test copy, and warns against treating the strategy as guaranteed profit. The cited promotion offers more instruction; it does not claim that enrollment or running the bot will produce returns.
